newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new national library named for Mitterrand.
newsitem.headline: France's new national library named for Mitterrand.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac will name France's new national library after late president Francois Mitterrand, who chose to build the glass and steel complex in a dusty corner of southeastern Paris, Chirac aides said on Monday.
Chirac will personally inaugurate the new library on December 17, the presidential aides said.

Mitterrand, a great lover of books who died in January, eight months after completing two seven-year terms as head of state, chose the new library as one of the major public works projects of his presidency.

The sleek complex, consisting of four L-shaped glass towers surrounding a sunken urban "forest" -- the whole nestling in a maze of railway tracks and roadways -- cost 30 billion francs ($6 billion), far above initial projections.
Mitterrand was asked during one of the last televised interviews of his presidency whether he wanted the controversial edifice named after him. "Why?" he responded curtly.

Later in the interview, he reluctantly conceded that the "Francois Mitterrand Library" would not be such a bad name. But he added: "If you were charged with the decision and you asked me to take that decision, I would tell you no."

Mitterrand also acknowledged during the April 1995 interview that he had rushed construction of the four glass towers so they would be too far along to be torn down when voters threw out France's Socialist government in 1993 general elections.
Officials said the new library would hold only 180,000 reference books -- a tiny fraction of the existing national library's collection -- when it opens its doors to the public on December 20.
Next to be moved over from the old building would be periodicals and rarely used books, a process expected to take 18 months.
Only in January 1998 would workers begin to transfer the 10 million volumes that make up the current library's core collection, they said.

Some designers ridiculed the new library because its glass towers required the addition of costly protection for the books from sunlight and heat. It will also need a staff of 2,700 people compared to just 500 to run the existing neoclassical building in the capital's second district.
Admirers countered that the new library would be more "democratic" than the overcrowded building it replaces, which is open to only a limited number of scholars.

Chirac's office said the old library, located between the Rue de Richelieu and the Rue Vivienne to the north of the Palais Royal, would be renamed after Cardinal Richelieu, chief minister to King Louis XIII.
